newsitem.title: CANADA: Out of the closet and into the blue.
newsitem.headline: Out of the closet and into the blue.

text.p: Perhaps it is time for more than a few of us to come out of the closet on this one.
"Yep, I too was beat by a computer playing chess." We could sing this from the cover of Time; we could tell our friends; we could be frank with our parents.
But thanks to Garry Kasparov and his humbling defeat before a hulking machine, we can all be honest and open.

There has been much outpouring since humans were humbled before a great big bad machine made up of silicon, blinking lights and a power cord. Kasparov, the five-foot 10-inch Chess dynamo threw in the towel after an "epic struggle" in early May against a six-foot five-inch, 1.4 ton computer called Deep Blue.

Much weeping and gnashing of teeth in the media followed the defeat, with commentary mostly along the lines that we the human race, once the lords over everything, must now consider stepping aside for a greater force.
"In a match like this there are many discoveries, and one of them is that sometimes the computer plays very human moves," Kasparov said after the fourth game.

MSNBC columnist Joan Connell wrote, "And even though Deep Blue is probably a more sophisticated thinker than your average college sophomore, it can never dip into the deep pool of human passion, mystery, innocence and experience that is at the heart of artistic creativity. Or can it?"
Or can it? That's what's driving everybody crazy. Have we finally created the Frankenstein of technology that will now cut loose and rule the planet?

If we were honest -- and this is the perfect time to come clean -- many of us could admit that we have been humbled well before this. I sort of remember my moment of truth, although it is natural to suppress these kinds of experiences. Perhaps lacking in friends, I challenged my computer to a single game of chess using some off-the-shelf game software.

It was a struggle, though not necessarily epic, but in the end I lost to the dang thing. I believe the machine was packing a whopping 286 chip (that's a few generations before today's trendy Pentium chip for any of you young readers) and I'm sure that computer could analyze several chess board positions in an hour, or about triple anything I could throw at it.

I don't remember hanging my head in shame, a la Kasparov, but maybe (and I'm being dreadfully honest again here) that was because it was not the first or the last time I have been humbled by a machine.
In fact each time I've attempted to record a late night movie on my VCR and came up with a test pattern instead of the film with all the subtitles, I have been humbled.

Each time my state-or-the-art laptop computer froze for no apparent reason and refused to obey me, I've been humbled. Each time my computer interrupted my work with the chilling "this program has performed an illegal operation," I've been humbled.

Of course these problems you and I have with machines are due to our own failings. If the Deep Blue triumph over Kasparov taught us anything it was that machines are infallible and ready to step in and take over their top position in the natural pecking order.

In Toronto's Financial Post, writer Andrew Clark argued that the loss illustrated that man with the creation of machines has finally overcome what God has created in the singular human. He belives that soon or later your computer will cease to be separate from you but become a necessary attachment.
"In the 21st century, no man will be an island -- he will have to have some mechanical parts," Clark wrote.

As for me, I can't wait to head over to the computer parts depot for humans. "Yes, I'll take one of those Pentium IV's, hold the flaws, and definitely lather on some of that parallel processing for the old cranium."
And then if anything goes wrong, we know the machine will take of it: "This body has performed an illegal operation and will be shut down."
